newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone coup leader was freed in jailbreak.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone coup leader was freed in jailbreak.

text.p: Sierra Leone's new leader Major Johnny Paul Koromah was in jail on treason charges until soldiers stormed Freetown's Pademba Road prison early on Sunday.

By the end of the day he had gone on state radio to present himself as head of state and leader of the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) and demand the return of rebel leader Foday Sankoh to join the government.
Koromah, 33, is the highest ranking officer among the coup leaders, but is less well known in Sierra Leone than AFRC spokesman Captain Paul Thomas.
Koromah was arrested last year in western Sierra Leone, where he was commanding troops deployed to deter rebel attacks, in connection with an alleged coup attempt last September.

Officials said ousted civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, whose elected government took over from military rulers in March 1996, was to have been killed in the coup attempt. Five soldiers were detained over the foiled attempt.
Koromah received military training in Nigeria and, like the leaders of the 1994 coup in Gambia, in Britain.
He is a northern Limba, the same ethnic group as former president Joseph Momoh, who was ousted in a coup in 1992 and recently returned home from exile in neighbouring Guinea.
Many northerners resented what they saw as domination of the civilian government by southern Mendes like Kabbah.
The army was also angered by the president's reliance on civilian Kamajor militias to protect mining areas in the southeast.

In an interview on BBC Africa Service radio on Tuesday, Kabbah said his one regret was rejecting the advice of his aides for a summary trial of Koromah "which could have led to execution". Kabbah, a lawyer by training, opted for due process.
One report said Koromah had been due to appear in court on Monday, the day after he seized power. Nine suspects pleaded not guilty to treason charges in the case last December.

In his first radio broadcast on Sunday night, Koromah said he had seized power because the the government had failed to consolidate a peace deal with Sankoh's rebels and the political situation had been nurturing tribal conflict.
